source.title: Sharp feature-learning transitions and Bayes-optimal neural scaling laws in extensive-width networks

record.file_problem: Full text is present; equations and some symbols have minor extraction/formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: Tests power-law generalization-error scaling in a synthetic teacher–student knowledge-transfer setting, rather than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study reports Bayes-optimal and A DAM-trained student generalization-error scaling in its own teacher–student setting. It does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, token/compute scaling, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture-shape effects, or downstream-task performance. Values used only to select student width and results cited from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study is a theory paper on a synthetic one-hidden-layer teacher–student network with Gaussian inputs and MSE error. It derives power laws in data size, and shows them empirically, for a Bayes-optimal student and an ADAM-trained student (k=100, d=200). None of these are language models, models of another real modality (image, video), or repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer regimes of real pretrained models. The behaviour is power-law error scaling, but the kind of system differs from what every version names, so the results go under fits_no_version rather than testing V5. r1 and r2 are analytic derivations from heuristic cavity equations, not measurements of trained systems.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that, in an extensive-width one-hidden-layer teacher–student model, sequential sharp feature-learning transitions define an effective width kc. For β>1/2, kc unifies two Bayes-optimal data-size regimes as εBO=Θ(kc d/n). An ADAM student near kc tracks these exponents up to a small gap on the weakest features. The derivation is heuristic, and the model-size exponent 1−2β for ADAM students is argued, not proven.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives and numerically evaluates Bayes-optimal mean-square generalization error and trains a one-hidden-layer student on synthetic teacher-generated data. It does not use language-model pretraining cross-entropy or the original language-model scaling-law procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported student scaling depends on student width relative to the critical/effective width and on whether the data regime is feature-learning or refinement. The paper also reports a residual algorithmic gap for the weakest features under A DAM.

fits_no_version.finding: In a synthetic extensive-width teacher–student network with power-law readout (β>1/2), Bayes-optimal error scales as n^{1/(2β)−1}, then as n^{-1} once all features are learnable. ADAM students near the effective width track these exponents, except about 5% of the weakest features stay unlearned at large n.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toy/theoretical models: neural power-law error scaling with data arises from sequential feature learning, with a crossover to the parametric n^-1 rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Toy ADAM student error follows ks^{1−2β} below a critical width. Error rises beyond that width as wider students overfit unlearnable features (Fig. 1 middle).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toy/theoretical models: model-size power law with a data-dependent optimal width, beyond which error increases.

record.problems: The main derivation is heuristic and relies on unproved cavity-field and overlap-concentration assumptions; the authors state that the HMC simulations do not validate the prediction of effective width kc. The empirical example is small (d = 200, k = 100, 9 runs in Figure 1), and the refinement-regime A DAM result has a residual algorithmic gap.
record.rows_left_out: None of the qualifying scaling outcomes were left out. Figure 1's selected widths from a grid search are not recorded as separate results because the width choices themselves are hyperparameter-selection outcomes.

untested.parts: Held-out LM pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small to large runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The authors list characterizing it as future work.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes of real models.
Dependence of fitted LM exponents and allocations on setup and fitting choices.

missing.what: Non-monotone model-size behaviour: test error increases beyond a critical student width (Fig. 1 middle and left; reduced-width student beats full width at n/(kd)=2).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/tests classification and its V5 supports/limits_scope labels are dropped. V5 names real modalities and training regimes of real models, not synthetic Gaussian-input toy networks. HMC simulations validate the overlaps but not the kc prediction itself (Appendix K.2).

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy of language models and scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Loss-minimizing parameter and token counts under a fixed compute budget, and their growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities; repeated-data, fine-tuning, and other transfer settings beyond this synthetic teacher–student setting.
Downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and systematic departures from a single power law.
